title: Pressures in the Body
lead: Every pressure a physician measures is a gauge pressure, and the most common of all medical examinations is a reading of the pressure in the arteries. This section takes the pressures of the body in turn: the blood pressure that rises in the feet of a standing person by the weight of the column of blood below the heart, the pressure that holds the eye in shape and the force it becomes when glaucoma raises it, the pressure inside the lungs that swings below and above atmospheric with each breath, the fluid that floats the brain, the bladder and its reflex, and the largest pressures of all, between the vertebrae of the spine.
objectives: Explain the concept of pressure the in human body.
Explain systolic and diastolic blood pressures.
Describe pressures in the eye, lungs, spinal column, bladder, and skeletal system.
summary_html:
• Measuring blood pressure is among the most common of all medical examinations.
  • The pressures in various parts of the body can be measured and often provide valuable medical indicators.
  • The shape of the eye is maintained by fluid pressure, called intraocular pressure.
  • When the circulation of fluid in the eye is blocked, it can lead to a buildup in pressure, a condition called glaucoma.
  • Some of the other pressures in the body are spinal and skull pressures, bladder pressure, pressures in the skeletal system.

figures.original_caption: Schematic of the circulatory system showing typical pressures. The two pumps in the heart increase pressure and that pressure is reduced as the blood flows through the body. Long-term deviations from these pressures have medical implications discussed in some detail in the Fluid Dynamics and Its Biological and Medical Applications. Only aortal or arterial blood pressure can be measured noninvasively.

(a) During inhalation, muscles expand the chest, and the diaphragm moves downward, reducing pressure inside the lungs to less than atmospheric (negative gauge pressure). Pressure between the lungs and chest wall is even lower to overcome the positive pressure created by surface tension in the lungs. (b) During gentle exhalation, the muscles simply relax and surface tension in the alveoli creates a positive pressure inside the lungs, forcing air out. Pressure between the chest wall and lungs remains negative to keep them attached to the chest wall, but it is less negative than during inhalation.

exercises.prompt: During forced exhalation, such as when blowing up a balloon, the diaphragm and chest muscles create a pressure of 60.0 mm Hg between the lungs and chest wall. What force in newtons does this pressure create on the $600\ \text{cm}^2$ surface area of the diaphragm?

answer.hint: Convert the pressure to N/m² with 1.0 mm Hg = 133 N/m² and the area to m², then the force is $\kF = \kPr A$.

exercises.prompt: One way to force air into an unconscious person’s lungs is to squeeze on a balloon appropriately connected to the subject. What force must you exert on the balloon with your hands to create a gauge pressure of 4.00 cm water, assuming you squeeze on an effective area of $50.0\ \text{cm}^2$?

answer.hint: A gauge pressure of 4.00 cm of water is the pressure at the bottom of a column of water 4.00 cm tall, $\kPg = \kh\krho\kg$; the force on the balloon is that pressure times the area of your hands.

exercises.prompt: Heroes in movies hide beneath water and breathe through a hollow reed (villains never catch on to this trick). In practice, you cannot inhale in this manner if your lungs are more than 60.0 cm below the surface. What is the maximum negative gauge pressure you can create in your lungs on dry land, assuming you can achieve $-3.00\ \text{cm}$ water pressure with your lungs 60.0 cm below the surface?

answer.hint: Under water, the water presses on your chest with a gauge pressure of 60.0 cm of water, and your lungs must be pulled 3.00 cm of water below that to draw air in through the reed. On dry land the same muscles pull against the atmosphere alone.

exercises.prompt: A full-term fetus typically has a mass of 3.50 kg. (a) What pressure does the weight of such a fetus create if it rests on the mother’s bladder, supported on an area of $90.0\ \text{cm}^2$? (b) Convert this pressure to millimeters of mercury and determine if it alone is great enough to trigger the micturition reflex (it will add to any pressure already existing in the bladder).

parts.hint: The force is the weight of the fetus, $m\kg$, and the pressure is that weight divided by the area in m².
Divide by 133 N/m² per mm Hg, and compare with the 25 mm Hg at which the reflex is triggered.

answer.solution: (a) $3.81\times 10^{3}\ \text{N/m}^2$ (b) 28.7 mm Hg, which is sufficient to trigger micturition reflex

figure.caption: A water manometer used to measure pressure in the spinal fluid. The height of the fluid in the manometer is measured relative to the spinal column, and the manometer is open to the atmosphere. The measured pressure will be considerably greater if the person sits up.

exercises.prompt: Pressure in the spinal fluid is measured as shown in the figure. If the pressure in the spinal fluid is 10.0 mm Hg: (a) What is the reading of the water manometer in cm water? (b) What is the reading if the person sits up, placing the top of the fluid 60 cm above the tap? The fluid density is 1.05 g/mL.

parts.hint: The manometer reads the gauge pressure as the height of a water column, $\kPg = \kh\krho\kg$ with the density of water. Convert 10.0 mm Hg to N/m² first.
Sitting up puts a column of spinal fluid 60 cm tall above the tap, and its weight adds to the pressure the manometer reads. Its density is 1.05 g/mL, not that of water.

exercises.prompt: During heavy lifting, a disk between spinal vertebrae is subjected to a 5000-N compressional force. (a) What pressure is created, assuming that the disk has a uniform circular cross section 2.00 cm in radius? (b) What deformation is produced if the disk is 0.800 cm thick and has a Young’s modulus of $1.5\times 10^{9}\ \text{N/m}^2$?

parts.hint: The area of the disk is $\pi r^2$ with $r = 2.00\ \text{cm}$ in meters, and the pressure is $\kF/A$.
The change in thickness is $\Delta L = \frac{1}{Y}\frac{\kF}{A}L_0$, with the pressure of part (a) standing for $\kF/A$ and $L_0$ the thickness of the disk.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you hit a steel nail with a 0.500-kg hammer, initially moving at $15.0\ \text{m/s}$ and brought to rest in 2.80 mm. (a) What average force is exerted on the nail? (b) How much is the nail compressed if it is 2.50 mm in diameter and 6.00-cm long? (c) What pressure is created on the 1.00-mm-diameter tip of the nail?

parts.hint: The hammer stops in 2.80 mm, so its average acceleration follows from $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax$, and the average force is the hammer’s mass times that acceleration.
The nail is compressed along its length by $\Delta L = \frac{1}{Y}\frac{\kF}{A}L_0$, with the area of its 2.50 mm shaft and Young’s modulus for steel.
The tip is a circle 1.00 mm across, so its area is $\pi(0.500\ \text{mm})^2$ in m², and the pressure is the force of part (a) over that area.

exercises.prompt: You are pumping up a bicycle tire with a hand pump, the piston of which has a 2.00-cm radius. (a) What force in newtons must you exert to create a pressure of $6.90\times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ (b) What is unreasonable about this (a) result? (c) Which premises are unreasonable or inconsistent?

answer.hint: The force is the pressure times the area of the piston, $\kF = \kPr A$ with $A = \pi r^2$. Then ask whether a person can push that hard on a hand pump.
answer.solution: (a) 867 N (b) This is too much force to exert with a hand pump. (c) The assumed radius of the pump is too large; it would be nearly two inches in diameter—too large for a pump or even a master cylinder. The pressure is reasonable for bicycle tires.
